passages.title: The New Boy
text: The new boy arrived in the third week of term, which is the worst possible time.

By the third week, everybody already has somebody to sit with at recess. The seats are decided. Mrs Ong put him at the empty desk beside mine, said his name was Arjun, and went back to the whiteboard.
For four days, Arjun said nothing at all except "yes" and "thank you".

At recess he sat at the end of the long table with his lunchbox and ate very slowly, one thing at a time, looking at the wall. I watched him from two tables away, where I sat with Wei Jie and Faizal, and I thought about going over, and then the bell rang, and then it was the next day.
This happened four times.
On the Friday, Wei Jie was away with a fever, and Faizal had a dental appointment, and at recess I found myself standing in the middle of the canteen holding a tray with nowhere obvious to go.
So I sat down opposite Arjun, because it was that or eat standing up.
He looked up. Then he pushed his box of biscuits into the middle of the table, which I understood to mean that I could take one.

It turned out that Arjun had moved from Chennai six weeks earlier, that he had an older sister who was already at secondary school, and that he could name every bone in the human hand. He showed me on my own hand, pressing each knuckle and saying a word I could not repeat.
We talked until the bell went.
On Monday, Wei Jie came back, and the four of us sat together, and by the end of term I could not remember what the seating had been like before.

I still think about those four days, though. I had wanted to go over the whole time. What stopped me was not unkindness. It was that going over would have meant walking across the canteen on my own while people watched, and at nine years old that felt like a great deal to ask.
It took a fever and a dental appointment to make me brave.

questions.q: Why does the narrator say the third week is "the worst possible time" to arrive?
questions.a: Because by then everybody has already made friends and decided where they sit at recess, so there is no easy way for a newcomer to join a group.
questions.tip: The reason is explained in paragraph 2. Reword it.

questions.q: How do we know that Arjun was lonely during his first four days?
questions.a: He barely spoke, saying only 'yes' and 'thank you', and at recess the narrator sat alone at the end of the long table eating slowly and staring at the wall.
questions.tip: Give the evidence, not just the conclusion.

questions.q: What made the narrator finally sit with Arjun?
questions.a: His two usual friends were both absent that Friday, so the narrator was left standing in the canteen with a tray and nowhere else to sit.
questions.tip: It was not a decision to be kind — say what actually happened.

questions.q: What did Arjun mean by pushing his biscuits into the middle of the table?
questions.a: He was offering to share them, which was his way of welcoming the narrator without having to say anything.
questions.tip: Explain the gesture, then say why it mattered.

questions.q: Give two things the narrator learnt about Arjun that day.
questions.a: Any two of: the narrator had moved from Chennai six weeks earlier; the narrator had an older sister already at secondary school; the narrator could name every bone in the human hand.
questions.tip: Two facts are asked for. Any two of the three will do.

questions.q: "This happened four times." Why is this short sentence effective?
questions.a: Its shortness makes the repetition feel heavy and deliberate, and it shows that the narrator missed the same chance again and again rather than only once.
questions.tip: Comment on both the form and what it tells us.

questions.q: The narrator says "What stopped me was not unkindness." What did stop him?
questions.a: Firstly, the narrator would have had to cross the canteen by himself. In addition, other pupils would have watched him do it. Finally, at nine years old that kind of public attention felt frightening, so his fear of being noticed outweighed his wish to be kind.
questions.tip: Three marks. The third point is about how a nine-year-old feels, not what happened.

questions.q: Explain the last line: "It took a fever and a dental appointment to make me brave."
questions.a: Firstly, the narrator is admitting that the narrator did not choose to be brave — two accidents forced him into it. In addition, the ordinariness of a fever and a dental appointment makes his own courage sound very small by comparison. Finally, the line is gently self-critical, showing that as an older narrator the narrator can see how easily the friendship might never have happened.
questions.tip: Three marks. Notice the humour and the self-criticism together.

questions.q: Which word in the passage means 'cruelty'?
questions.a: 'Unkindness'.
questions.tip: Look in the last paragraph.

questions.q: Find a word in the passage that means 'clear to see, without needing to be told'.
questions.a: 'Obvious'.
questions.tip: It describes how plain something was.

passages.title: Why Some Animals Play Dead
text: When an opossum is threatened, it does not run away. It falls over, opens its mouth, lets its tongue hang out and stops moving. It can stay like this for up to four hours.

This behaviour is often called playing dead, but the name is misleading. The animal is not pretending. Scientists have found that the opossum's heart rate drops sharply and that it becomes genuinely unable to move. It is closer to fainting than to acting.

The strategy works because of how predators hunt. Many hunting animals are triggered by movement, and a great many will not eat something they did not kill themselves, because an animal that is already dead may be diseased. A motionless opossum is therefore both harder to notice and less appetising.

Opossums are not alone. Certain snakes roll onto their backs. Some beetles fold their legs and drop from leaves. A few species of frog do it. So do some fish. The behaviour has appeared separately in many unrelated animals, which suggests it works well enough to be worth evolving more than once.

It is not without cost. An animal lying still cannot feed, cannot escape a second attacker and cannot protect its young. Some opossums have been run over because they froze in the road rather than moving. The strategy only makes sense against a predator that hunts by sight and movement, and it is useless against one that hunts by smell.
There is also a limit to how long it can last. An opossum in this state slowly recovers whether or not the danger has passed, and a young opossum recovers faster than an adult.
Like most things in nature, then, it is not a perfect defence. It is simply one that works often enough.

questions.q: Describe what an opossum does when it is threatened.
questions.a: It collapses onto the ground with its mouth open and its tongue hanging out, and remains completely still, sometimes for as long as four hours.
questions.tip: Include the detail and the duration.

questions.q: Why does the writer say that the name 'playing dead' is misleading?
questions.a: Because the animal is not deliberately pretending — its heart rate falls sharply and it genuinely cannot move, so the state is more like fainting than acting.
questions.tip: Two marks: what people assume, and what actually happens.

questions.q: Give two reasons why lying still protects the opossum from predators.
questions.a: Firstly, many predators are triggered by movement, so a still animal is less likely to be noticed. Secondly, many hunters avoid eating animals they did not kill themselves, in case the carcass is diseased.
questions.tip: Two distinct reasons from paragraph 3.

questions.q: What does the word 'motionless' mean in paragraph 3?
questions.a: Not moving at all.
questions.tip: A short synonym is enough for one mark.

questions.q: Why does the writer mention snakes, beetles, frogs and fish?
questions.a: To show that the behaviour has developed independently in many unrelated kinds of animal, which suggests it must be an effective defence.
questions.tip: Do not just list them — say why the list is there.

questions.q: Give two disadvantages of this strategy.
questions.a: Any two of: it cannot feed while it lies still; it cannot escape if a second attacker arrives; it cannot protect its young; it is useless against a predator that hunts by smell.
questions.tip: Two disadvantages are asked for. Any two will do.

questions.q: Why are some opossums run over on roads?
questions.a: Because their instinct is to freeze when they sense danger, so they stop moving in the middle of the road instead of running clear of the vehicle.
questions.tip: Link the behaviour to the outcome.

questions.q: Explain the final sentence: "It is simply one that works often enough."
questions.a: Firstly, the writer is admitting that the defence fails in many situations. In addition, it does not need to succeed every time to be worth having — it only needs to work more often than it fails. Finally, the sentence sums up the whole passage's balanced view, that a natural defence is judged by how useful it usually is rather than by whether it is perfect.
questions.tip: Three marks. The last point is about the writer's overall attitude.

questions.q: Which word in the passage means 'not moving at all'?
questions.a: 'Motionless'.
questions.tip: Look in the paragraph describing what the animal's body does.

questions.q: Find a word in the passage that means 'set off automatically, without being chosen'.
questions.a: 'Triggered'.
questions.tip: It describes how the response begins.

passages.title: The Wrong Trophy
text: The trophy said MEI LING TAN, and my name is Mei Ling Tang.

I noticed in the car on the way home, turning it over in my lap while my mother talked about what we would have for dinner. One letter. It had been engraved in gold on a small black plate, and whoever had typed it had left off the g.
"They spelt it wrong," I said.
My mother glanced at it at a traffic light. "So they did. Never mind. Everyone knows it's yours."

But here is the thing. There is a Mei Ling Tan in Primary Five. She plays the erhu. She had also been at the prize-giving, because she won something for music, and her trophy had been handed out from the same table by the same teacher.
I did not say this to my mother.
For two days the trophy sat on the shelf above my desk, and every time I looked up it said somebody else's name.
On Wednesday I took it to the general office and explained. The lady behind the counter, Mrs Selvam, looked at it, then looked at a list, and then made a small noise.
It turned out that Mei Ling Tan's trophy said MEI LING TANG.
She had noticed on the first night and said nothing, because she assumed it was hers and that somebody had simply added a letter. She had been looking at my name for two days while I looked at hers.
Mrs Selvam swapped the little black plates over with a screwdriver in about ninety seconds.

We met in the corridor afterwards, both holding the correct trophy at last, and we stood there for a moment not quite knowing what to say. Then she said, "Two days," and I said, "Two days," and we both laughed in a way that was slightly too loud for a corridor.
I do not know her well even now. But we nod at each other, and it is a particular kind of nod, and neither of us has ever explained it to anybody.

questions.q: What was wrong with the narrator's trophy?
questions.a: It bore the name MEI LING TAN, not her own name MEI LING TANG. The plate on her trophy was in fact the other girl's name plate.
questions.tip: One mark, so keep it short and precise.

questions.q: How did the narrator's mother react, and what does this show about her?
questions.a: She glanced at it briefly at a traffic light and said it did not matter because everyone knew the trophy was her daughter's. This shows that she saw it as a trivial mistake not worth worrying about.
questions.tip: Answer both halves — what she did and what it reveals.

questions.q: Why did the mistake matter more to the narrator than to her mother?
questions.a: Firstly, there was a real Mei Ling Tan at the school, so the name on the trophy belonged to an actual other person. In addition, the narrator saw the wrong name every time she looked up from her desk, so it troubled her daily. Finally, it made the trophy feel as though it were not really hers.
questions.tip: Three marks. The first point is the one the mother did not know.

questions.q: Why do you think the narrator did not tell her mother about the other Mei Ling?
questions.a: Because her mother had already dismissed the problem, and explaining would have meant arguing about something her mother thought was unimportant — so it was easier to deal with it herself.
questions.tip: 'Why do you think' — this is inference, not stated.

questions.q: What had happened to the two trophies?
questions.a: The engraving plates had been swapped by mistake, so the narrator's trophy carried the other girl's name and the other girl's trophy carried hers.
questions.tip: Two marks: state the mix-up clearly in your own words.

questions.q: Why had Mei Ling Tan not reported the mistake?
questions.a: Because she assumed the trophy was hers and that somebody had simply added a letter to her name by accident, so she did not realise anything was wrong.
questions.tip: Look at what each girl does once the mistake is discovered, not at what either of them says.

questions.q: Explain why the two girls laughed "in a way that was slightly too loud for a corridor".
questions.a: Firstly, they had both spent two days privately bothered by the same odd problem without knowing the other existed. In addition, the coincidence was genuinely funny once it was explained. Finally, the loudness suggests relief as much as amusement — each had been carrying a small worry alone and suddenly found somebody who understood it exactly.
questions.tip: Three marks. Save the point about relief for last.

questions.q: Explain the last paragraph, and why it is a good ending.
questions.a: Firstly, it admits honestly that the two girls did not become close friends, which is more believable than a neat friendship ending. In addition, the shared nod shows that one small experience can connect two people permanently even without conversation. Finally, the detail that neither has ever explained it to anybody makes the moment feel private and valuable, which is a quieter and more memorable close than a dramatic one.
questions.tip: Three marks. Comment on the honesty of the ending as well as its meaning.

questions.q: Which word in the passage means 'exchanged one for the other'?
questions.a: 'Swapped'.
questions.tip: Look at what turned out to have happened to the two name plates.

questions.q: Find a word in the passage that means 'took for granted without checking'.
questions.a: 'Assumed'.
questions.tip: It describes what the narrator did about the engraving.

passages.title: The Case Against Bottled Water
text: Singapore has some of the cleanest tap water in the world. It is tested continuously, it meets international drinking standards, and it costs roughly one-thousandth of the price of the same volume sold in a plastic bottle. And yet bottled water sales continue to rise.

The usual explanation is convenience, and there is truth in that. A bottle can be bought anywhere and carried away. But convenience does not explain the whole picture, because a refillable bottle is also portable and there are now water coolers in most malls, MRT stations and schools.

A better explanation is habit. People buy bottled water because they have always bought it, because it is displayed at every counter, and because carrying a bottle of something is easier than remembering to bring one.

The environmental cost is well known. A plastic bottle takes a few minutes to drink and several centuries to break down. Fewer than half are recycled, and even those that are usually become a lower-grade plastic that cannot be made into a bottle again.

What is less often mentioned is the cost of moving water around. Bottled water is heavy, and much of it is transported considerable distances by road or sea, which uses fuel to deliver something that already comes out of a tap a few metres away.

There is a second cost that rarely appears on any label. Producing the plastic for a single one-litre bottle uses roughly three litres of water, most of it in the factory rather than in the bottle. A drink sold on the promise of purity therefore costs several times its own volume before it reaches a shelf.

There are exceptions, and an honest argument must acknowledge them. In an emergency, or in places where the tap water is genuinely unsafe, bottled water saves lives. Some people are advised by a doctor to drink water with a particular mineral content. These are real reasons.
But they do not describe most purchases. Most bottles are bought by someone who walked past a water cooler on the way to the shop.

The solution is neither dramatic nor new. A refillable bottle costs a few dollars and lasts for years. The difficulty has never been the technology. It has been remembering to pick it up on the way out of the door.

questions.q: Give two facts the writer uses to show that Singapore's tap water is good.
questions.a: It is tested continuously and meets international standards for drinking water, and it costs around a thousand times less than the same amount of bottled water.
questions.tip: Two separate facts from paragraph 1.

questions.q: Why does the writer say that convenience "does not explain the whole picture"?
questions.a: Because a refillable bottle is just as easy to carry, and water coolers are now available in most malls, MRT stations and schools, so buying a bottle is not the only convenient option.
questions.tip: The counter-argument is in the same paragraph.

questions.q: In your own words, explain what the writer means by habit.
questions.a: People buy bottled water without really thinking about it, because they have always done so, because it is on sale everywhere they look, and because it takes less effort than planning ahead.
questions.tip: Do not lift 'displayed at every counter'.

questions.q: Explain why recycling does not fully solve the problem.
questions.a: Fewer than half of plastic bottles are recycled at all, and those that are usually become a poorer-quality plastic that cannot be turned back into a bottle.
questions.tip: Two marks: the low rate, and what happens to what is recycled.

questions.q: What point is the writer making about transport?
questions.a: That bottled water is heavy and is often carried long distances using fuel, which is wasteful when the same water is already available from a tap only a few metres away.
questions.tip: Say what the fact is and why it matters.

questions.q: Why does the writer include paragraph 6, about exceptions?
questions.a: Firstly, it acknowledges that bottled water is genuinely necessary in emergencies, where tap water is unsafe, or where a doctor has advised it. In addition, including these cases shows the writer is being fair rather than one-sided. Finally, it makes the main argument stronger, because a reader is more likely to accept a case that has admitted its own limits.
questions.tip: Three marks. The third point is about persuasive technique.

questions.q: Explain the sentence: "Most bottles are bought by someone who walked past a water cooler on the way to the shop."
questions.a: It means that the majority of purchases are not made out of necessity at all — the buyer had a free alternative available moments earlier and simply did not use it.
questions.tip: Explain what the sentence is really accusing people of.

questions.q: "The difficulty has never been the technology." What does the writer think the real difficulty is, and what does this suggest about the solution?
questions.a: Firstly, the writer says the real difficulty is remembering to take a refillable bottle when leaving the house. In addition, this means the obstacle is a matter of personal habit rather than cost or invention. Finally, it suggests the problem is solvable by anyone immediately, without waiting for new products.
questions.tip: Three marks. End with what the reader is meant to do about it.

questions.q: Which word in the passage means 'able to be filled again'?
questions.a: 'Refillable'.
questions.tip: Look in the paragraph about what to carry instead.

questions.q: Find a word in the passage that means 'large, worth taking seriously'.
questions.a: 'Considerable'.
questions.tip: It describes the distances the bottles travel.

passages.title: The Metronome
text: Mrs Arulappan never once told me I had played something well.
I studied piano with her for seven years, from the age of eight, in a flat that smelt of floor polish and had a metronome on top of the upright that she set going before I had taken my coat off.
Her method was the same every week. I played. She listened with her eyes closed. Then she named, without any preamble, the single thing that had gone wrong.
"Bar nine. You rushed because it was getting difficult."
"You are playing the left hand as though it were an accompaniment. It is not."
"That was faster. It was not better."

I hated it for about two years. My friends had teachers who put stickers on the page. At eleven I asked my mother whether I could change, and she said I could decide at the end of the year, and by the end of the year I had stopped asking, though I could not at the time have said why.

What I understood much later is that Mrs Arulappan was never withholding praise in order to push me. She simply did not consider praise to be information. She had one hour a week, and she spent all of it on the thing that would make the next week better.
In my final year she entered me for an examination I did not expect to pass. I passed it, with a mark that surprised both of us.
I went to her flat afterwards with the certificate. She read it, put it on the piano, and said, "Bar nine of the Chopin. You still rush."
Then she made me tea, which she had never done before in seven years, and we drank it without saying very much, and I understood that this was the entire celebration and that it was enough.

I asked her once, in my fifth year, why she never said anything was good. She thought about it for long enough that I wished I had not asked. Then she said that there were a great many people who would tell me I was wonderful, and that they would all be trying to be kind, and that being kind and being useful were not always the same errand. She said I had one hour a week with somebody whose only job was to be useful, and that she did not intend to waste it.
She died when I was twenty-six. I do not play often now, and when I do it is badly.
But I have taught four people things since — nothing to do with music — and every single time I have caught myself doing it her way. One hour. One thing that is wrong. No stickers.
I am aware that this makes me a difficult teacher. I have not been able to make myself stop.

questions.q: Describe Mrs Arulappan's teaching method.
questions.a: Every lesson she listened to him play with her eyes closed, then immediately named the one thing that had gone wrong, without any introduction or encouragement first.
questions.tip: Two marks: what she did, and how she did it.

questions.q: Why did the narrator hate the lessons at first?
questions.a: Because the narrator never received any praise, while his friends had teachers who rewarded them with stickers on the page, so his lessons felt harsher by comparison.
questions.tip: The comparison with his friends is the point.

questions.q: "That was faster. It was not better." What does this remark tell us about her standards?
questions.a: It shows she judged playing by its musical quality rather than by effort or speed, and that she would not accept an improvement in one thing as an excuse for a weakness in another.
questions.tip: Explain what she valued, not just what she said.

questions.q: Explain what the narrator means by "she did not consider praise to be information".
questions.a: Firstly, the narrator means she saw praise as telling a pupil nothing they could act on. In addition, she believed her limited hour was better spent identifying the fault that would improve the following week. Finally, this shows her silence was not coldness or a deliberate tactic, but a considered view of what teaching time was for.
questions.tip: Three marks. The last point corrects what the reader may have assumed.

questions.q: Why does the writer mention that the narrator stopped asking to change teachers "though I could not at the time have said why"?
questions.a: It shows that the narrator had begun to value her teaching before the narrator was old enough to understand what the narrator was getting from it, so his loyalty came from instinct rather than reasoning.
questions.tip: Focus on the gap between feeling and understanding.

questions.q: Why is her response to the certificate significant?
questions.a: Firstly, she did not congratulate him even on the day the narrator passed an examination neither of them had expected. In addition, she returned immediately to the same fault she had named for years, showing her standards did not relax for an occasion. Finally, it confirms that her approach was consistent rather than cruel, because she treated his success exactly as she had treated everything else.
questions.tip: Three marks. The third point is about consistency.

questions.q: Why does the tea matter so much to the narrator?
questions.a: Firstly, she had never made him tea in seven years, so it was completely out of character. In addition, because she never praised him in words, this small unusual act had to carry all of her approval. Finally, the narrator says it was 'the entire celebration and that it was enough', which shows the narrator had learnt to read her meaning without needing it spoken.
questions.tip: Three marks. Explain why a cup of tea can mean so much.

questions.q: Explain the last two paragraphs and what they reveal about her influence.
questions.a: Firstly, the narrator admits the narrator barely plays any more and plays badly, so her lasting effect was not musical. In addition, the narrator has copied her method exactly whenever the narrator has taught anyone anything — one hour, one fault, no rewards. Furthermore, the narrator acknowledges that this makes him a difficult teacher, so the narrator can see the cost of her approach as well as its value. Finally, 'I have not been able to make myself stop' shows the influence runs deeper than choice, which is a more honest measure of a teacher than any qualification.
questions.tip: The last point is about the force of 'I have not been able to make myself stop' — far stronger than simply saying he still does it.

questions.q: Which word in the passage means 'an introduction before getting to the point'?
questions.a: 'Preamble'.
questions.tip: It describes how the teacher began each lesson.

questions.q: Find a word in the passage that means 'keeping something back deliberately'.
questions.a: 'Withholding'.
questions.tip: It appears where the narrator explains what the teacher was doing.

passages.title: The Letter She Never Sent
text: We found it while clearing the flat, in the third drawer of the dressing table, underneath a tin of buttons.
It was addressed to a Mr Harold Tay at an address in Katong, and it had a stamp on it, and it had never been posted.

My mother turned it over twice. The envelope was not sealed. She looked at me, and I looked at her, and neither of us said the obvious thing, which was that my grandmother had been dead for eleven days and could not now be asked.
In the end we did not open it.

I want to record that accurately, because I have since told the story several times and I have noticed a temptation to make us seem more certain than we were. We stood there for a long while. My mother's thumb was inside the flap at one point. We did not open it, but it was close, and I am not sure the decision was noble so much as postponed.
We asked my aunt. She had never heard of Harold Tay.
We looked him up. There was a Harold Tay who had died in 2004, and a Harold Tay who ran a printing business until the nineties, and no way of knowing whether either of them was the one.
The letter is now in a box in my mother's wardrobe, still unopened, and it has been there for nine years.

Once, about four years ago, my mother took the box down and put it on the kitchen table, and we both sat and looked at it for perhaps ten minutes. Then she carried it back to the wardrobe without either of us saying anything. We have not mentioned that afternoon since, and I am not sure which of us decided.

I think about it more than I expected to. Not because I want to know what is in it — or rather, I do want to know, but that is not the interesting part. What I think about is that my grandmother wrote it, and stamped it, and then did not post it, and kept it for what must have been decades in a drawer she opened every day.
She had a hundred chances to throw it away. She had a hundred chances to post it.
She did neither, which is its own kind of answer, and I suspect it is the only one we are going to get.

My mother says that opening it now would tell us about my grandmother, but it would tell us nothing about the version of her who decided not to send it, and that the second one is the one we actually lost.
I have never been able to think of a good reply to that.

questions.q: Where and how was the letter found?
questions.a: It was found while the family was clearing out the flat, in the third drawer of the dressing table, underneath a tin of buttons.
questions.tip: Two marks means include the circumstances as well as the place.

questions.q: What two details show that the letter had been meant to be sent?
questions.a: It was addressed to a named person at a specific address in Katong, and it already had a stamp on it.
questions.tip: Two pieces of evidence.

questions.q: Why does the narrator insist on recording the moment "accurately"?
questions.a: Firstly, she has told the story several times since and has noticed herself being tempted to make the family sound more principled than they were. In addition, she admits her mother's thumb was inside the flap, so they came very close to opening it. Finally, she says the decision may have been postponed rather than noble, which shows she wants to be honest about her own motives rather than flattering.
questions.tip: Three marks. This paragraph is about honesty, not about the letter.

questions.q: What did the family find out about Harold Tay?
questions.a: Very little — an aunt had never heard of him, and a search turned up two different men of that name with no way of telling whether either was the right one.
questions.tip: Say what they found and why it did not help.

questions.q: The narrator says she wants to know what is in the letter, "but that is not the interesting part". What does she find more interesting?
questions.a: Firstly, she is more interested in the fact that her grandmother wrote and stamped the letter but never sent it. In addition, she kept it for decades in a drawer she opened every day, so the decision was made repeatedly rather than once. Finally, this makes the grandmother's choice itself the mystery, rather than the contents of the envelope.
questions.tip: Three marks. The repetition of the choice is the key point.

questions.q: Explain: "She had a hundred chances to throw it away. She had a hundred chances to post it."
questions.a: It means she could easily have destroyed the letter or sent it at any time over many years, so keeping it unsent must have been deliberate rather than an oversight.
questions.tip: Explain why the writer puts the two options side by side.

questions.q: What does the mother mean by "the second one is the one we actually lost"?
questions.a: Firstly, she means that reading the letter would reveal facts about the grandmother's life. In addition, it would not explain the woman who chose year after year not to send it. Finally, that version of her grandmother — her reasons, her hesitation — is the part that died with her and that no letter can bring back.
questions.tip: Three marks. Distinguish the two 'versions' clearly.

questions.q: Why is "I have never been able to think of a good reply to that" an effective last line?
questions.a: Firstly, it ends the passage without resolving anything, which matches a story about a question that cannot be answered. In addition, it shows the narrator accepts her mother's reasoning even though she still wants to open the letter. Furthermore, the admission that she has no reply is more convincing than agreement would be, because it shows the pull she still feels. Finally, the line quietly tells the reader that the letter will probably stay closed, without the narrator having to say so.
questions.tip: Four marks. The final point is about what the line implies rather than states.

questions.q: Which word in the passage means 'the wish to do something you know you should not'?
questions.a: 'Temptation'.
questions.tip: It appears where the narrator is holding the envelope.

questions.q: Find a word in the passage that means 'put off until a later time'.
questions.a: 'Postponed'.
questions.tip: It describes what was done again and again.

passages.title: The Egg in the Drain
text: On Saturday morning, my sister Nadia and I heard a noise outside our flat.
It was a small sound. It went cheep, then stopped, then cheep again.
We looked over the corridor railing. We looked behind the bicycles. We looked under the letter boxes. We could not find it anywhere.
Then Nadia lay flat on the floor and put her ear against the drain cover.
"It is in here," she said.
The drain cover was a metal grid with narrow slots. Through them we could see something small and grey. It was a baby bird, and it could not get out.
I tried to lift the cover. It was far too heavy. We tried together, and it did not move at all.
"We need an adult," Nadia said.
Our father was asleep, because he had worked at night. Our mother had gone to the market. So we knocked on the door next to ours.
Uncle Ravi opened it, holding a newspaper. We told him about the bird. He looked through the slots, then went back inside without a word.
For a moment I thought he did not care.
Then he came back with a screwdriver and a torch.
It took him five minutes to lift the cover. Nadia held her jacket open like a net, Uncle Ravi guided the frightened bird into it, and then it was out.
We put it in a shoebox. Uncle Ravi telephoned the bird rescue centre, and a lady came at four o'clock and took the box away.
She told us it was a mynah chick. She said it would be fed every two hours and released when it could fly.
That evening our father asked what we had done all day.
Nadia said, "Nothing much."
I did not say anything either. But I still remember how heavy that drain cover was, and how light the bird was in the jacket.

questions.q: Where were Nadia and the narrator when they first heard the noise?
questions.a: They were at their flat, and the sound came from outside in the corridor.
questions.tip: Look at the first two paragraphs.

questions.q: Give two places the children searched before they found the bird.
questions.a: Any two of: over the corridor railing; behind the bicycles; under the letter boxes.
questions.tip: Two places are asked for. Any two will do.

questions.q: How did Nadia work out where the bird was?
questions.a: She lay down flat on the floor and put her ear against the drain cover.
questions.tip: She used her ears, not her eyes.

questions.q: Why could the children not rescue the bird by themselves?
questions.a: The metal drain cover was far too heavy for them to lift, even when they tried together.
questions.tip: Look at what happened when they both tried.

questions.q: Why did they go to Uncle Ravi instead of asking their own parents?
questions.a: Their father was asleep after working at night, and their mother had gone to the market.
questions.tip: Both parents are accounted for in the same paragraph.

questions.q: Why did the narrator think for a moment that Uncle Ravi did not care?
questions.a: Because he looked through the slots and went back inside without saying anything, so it seemed as though he was ignoring them. In fact he had gone to fetch a screwdriver and a torch.
questions.tip: Say what the narrator thought, and then what was really happening.

questions.q: What did Nadia do to help catch the bird?
questions.a: She held her jacket open like a net so that Uncle Ravi could guide the bird into it.
questions.tip: Look at the paragraph about lifting the cover.

questions.q: What two things did the lady from the rescue centre say would happen to the bird?
questions.a: It would be fed every two hours, and it would be released when it was able to fly.
questions.tip: Both facts are in the same short paragraph.

questions.q: Which word in the passage means 'thin openings'?
questions.a: 'Slots'.
questions.tip: It describes the gaps in the drain cover.

questions.q: The narrator remembers 'how heavy that drain cover was, and how light the bird was'. Why do you think he remembers those two things together?
questions.a: Because they are opposites, and putting them side by side shows how much effort went into saving something so small. It suggests that the size of the trouble was worth it.
questions.tip: Think about why a writer would put a heavy thing and a light thing in the same sentence.

passages.text:
The Umbrella Rule

My father has one rule about umbrellas, and he has never (1)______ from it in thirty years: you do not lend an umbrella, you give it.

The reasoning, as he explains it, is simple. A lent umbrella creates a small (2)______ between two people. The borrower must remember to return it; the lender must remember to ask. Both parties then spend several weeks slightly (3)______ of one another over an object worth eight dollars.

Giving it away removes all of that at a (4)______ .

I thought this was eccentric until I started counting. Our flat contains, at the last count, nine umbrellas. Six of them arrived because somebody gave one to my father during a (5)______ and he never gave it back, on the grounds that he had been given it rather than lent it.

The system, in other words, (6)______ itself. Umbrellas circulate around the neighbourhood, and nobody is ever (7)______ anybody anything.

Last month I was caught in a storm outside the library with a girl from my class who had no (8)______ . I offered her mine, and she said she would return it on Monday, and I heard myself say, "Don't. It's (9)______ ."

She looked at me strangely. I attempted to explain the rule and made a poor (10)______ of it, because it sounds far more sensible when my father says it.

On Monday she brought the umbrella back (11)______ , which rather defeated the purpose, and also a packet of biscuits, which did not.

I have since (12)______ that the rule does not entirely work. It relies on everybody understanding it, and almost nobody (13)______ .

But I have noticed something my father may not have intended. Because I no longer expect an umbrella (14)______ , I have stopped keeping any sort of mental account of who owes me what — and it turns out that (15)______ small account was costing me more attention than I realised.

The Last Bus Home

For six months of my first year at work, I caught the last bus home every night, and for six months I sat in the same (16)______ , three rows from the back on the left.

So did four other people. We never (17)______ . I do not know a single one of their names even now.

There was a woman in a nurse's uniform who slept with remarkable (18)______ and always woke one stop before her own. There was a man who did the crossword in pen. There was a student who ate the same packet of prawn crackers every night, and a very old gentleman who did nothing at all except look out of the (19)______ .

We were not friends. But over six months we became something, because in the second month the student fell asleep and (20)______ his stop, and the man with the crossword woke him without being asked, and after that we all (21)______ quietly looking out for one another.

When the nurse did not appear for a week, all four of us noticed. Nobody (22)______ it. When she came back, the old gentleman moved his bag off the seat beside him, which he had never done for (23)______ else, and she sat there, and that was the whole conversation.

I changed jobs in October and stopped taking that bus (24)______ .

I have thought about them a surprising amount since. We shared nothing except a (25)______ and a time of night. We knew nothing about each other's lives. And yet I would have done a great deal for any of them, and I am fairly (26)______ they would have done the same.

It has made me suspicious of the idea that you must know somebody (27)______ before you can look after them.

Most of the people who have helped me in my life have not known me (28)______ . They simply happened to be there, and noticed, and did the small (29)______ thing that was available to them.

I hope I have managed it myself occasionally, on some bus or other, without (30)______ .

answers.tip: He has never moved away from it.
They are slightly on guard with each other.
'At a stroke' means all at once.
When an umbrella would be needed.
'Nobody is ever owing anybody anything' — the money or favour is never outstanding.
He is giving it, not lending it.
She returned it despite what he said.
Referring back to the mental account.
She always woke at the same point.
They noticed but did not speak about it.
The modest thing they could do.
Without being aware of it himself.
